newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK November PSBR to show revenue fallback.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK November PSBR to show revenue fallback.

text.p: UK November public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) data on Tuesday are expected to show revenue growth dropping back sharply after a net repayment in October. The Reuters consensus forecast is for a budget deficit of 2.7 billion stg following a net repayment of 4.4 billion the previous month.
"It seems almost certain that receipts growth will fall back after the sharp jump in October," said Jonathan Loynes of HSBC Markets, who expects a PSBR of about 3.0 billion stg.
"In particular we expect the growth of VAT receipts to drop back into negative territory after the huge 47 percent figure recorded in October."

The fallback in receipt growth will be partly offset by the sale of the Ministry of Defence's housing, which is expected to raise 900 million stg, but this is the only special factor seen affecting the data.
"November is not a month for big movement on either side of the government's balance sheets. There's only the sale of MoD's married quarters." said David Philpotts at Schroders.
Schroders has forecast a 2.9 billion stg deficit.
Analysts said they expected the higher-than-expected repayment in October, plus strong economic growth and healthy revenue, to help the government attain its 26.4 billion stg deficit target for 1996.

"Although there may be some slippage on expenditure...and that's something which is difficult to avoid in the run-up to a general election...the receipt growth will be stronger than the government anticipates," said Ian Stewart at Merrill Lynch, who predicts a November shortfall of 2.0 billion stg.
Stewart added that government coffers could also be helped by new tax avoidance measures presented by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke in the November budget.
Economists at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell believe the government forecast of a 26.4 billion stg full-year deficit is too pessimistic.
"We look for a 25.5 billion stg deficit, with the difference mainly due to receipts," they wrote in their weekly comment.
